config.title: Multiple State Variables

intro.title: Multiple State Variables
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple counter app that tracks two separate values: a primary count and a secondary count. You will learn how to manage multiple independent pieces of state in a React component using the useState hook. The core concept is declaring and updating multiple state variables to handle different data points simultaneously. You will work with TypeScript to define types for your state, ensuring type safety. By the end, you'll understand how to structure components with several useState calls and update each state independently based on user interactions.
intro.usecase: Managing multiple state variables is essential for complex interactive interfaces like e-commerce product filters, where you need to track separate states for price range, selected categories, and sort order simultaneously. User profile forms require independent state management for name, email, password fields, and validation statuses. Dashboard components often maintain parallel states for data loading status, selected time ranges, and toggleable panel visibility. This pattern appears in virtually every production React application where UI elements need to respond independently to user interactions while maintaining coordinated functionality.

objectives: Initialize multiple independent state variables using useState in a React component
Apply distinct setter functions to update each state variable independently
Construct a component that renders multiple state values in the UI
Manipulate event handlers to control updates for different state variables
Integrate multiple state variables to manage separate pieces of component data
Configure a component to respond to user interactions by updating specific state variables
Implement a form or interface that binds inputs to multiple state values

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing modules in TypeScript
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary React APIs for using state in TypeScript are imported.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to import React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named CounterApp that returns a JSX element. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns a simple JSX element like a <div> or <h1>. Remember to use TypeScript syntax.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the CounterApp component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A CounterApp component is defined and returns a JSX element.
successCriteria: CounterApp component is defined and returns a JSX element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started defining the component, but make sure it's named CounterApp and returns a JSX element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Create a functional component named CounterApp that returns a JSX element.

steps.title: Initialize the first state variable
steps.instruction: Inside the CounterApp component, use useState to declare a state variable named 'count' initialized to 0.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial value 0 and destructure the returned array into count and setCount.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: state variable for a number
const [score, setScore] = useState(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a count state variable initialized to 0.
successCriteria: The component contains a useState call that declares a count variable initialized to 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with an initial value of 0 and naming the variable 'count'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use useState to create a state variable named count initialized to 0.

steps.title: Define the increment handler
steps.instruction: Inside your CounterApp component, create a function named handleIncrement that increments the count state variable using its setter function.
steps.hint: The function should call setCount with the new value. You can use the previous state to calculate the new count.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleIncrement function that properly updates the count state by incrementing it.
successCriteria: The handleIncrement function is defined, calls setCount, and correctly increments the count value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it properly increments the count using setCount.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleIncrement function is missing or doesn't correctly update the count state.

steps.title: Define the toggle handler
steps.instruction: Inside your CounterApp component, define a function named handleToggle that toggles the isActive state using its setter function.
steps.hint: You can toggle a boolean state by passing a function to the setter that returns the opposite of the current value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleToggle function that toggles the isActive state when called.
successCriteria: The handleToggle function is defined and uses the isActive state setter to toggle the boolean value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function is named handleToggle and properly toggles the isActive state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle handler isn't defined correctly. Check the function name and how you're updating the state.

steps.title: Add the main container structure
steps.instruction: In your CounterApp component, return a div container with a heading that says 'Multiple State Demo'.
steps.hint: Replace the current return statement with JSX that includes a div and an h1 element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a div containing an h1 with the text 'Multiple State Demo'.
successCriteria: The return statement includes a div element with an h1 child containing the text 'Multiple State Demo'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning a div with an h1 inside it, and the h1 text should be 'Multiple State Demo'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the return statement. You need to replace 'null' with a div containing an h1 element with the specified text.

steps.title: Display the count state and add increment button
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a paragraph element that displays the current count value and a button element with an onClick handler that calls the handleIncrement function.
steps.hint: Use JSX curly braces to display the count state variable inside the paragraph. The button should have an onClick attribute set to the handleIncrement function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show a paragraph displaying the current count value and a button that, when clicked, will increment the count.
successCriteria: Paragraph element displays the count state variable
Button element has onClick handler wired to handleIncrement function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both a paragraph showing the count value and a button with onClick={handleIncrement}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The required elements aren't present. Add a paragraph showing the count and a button with an onClick handler.

steps.title: Add conditional styling based on state
steps.instruction: Add a div wrapper around your existing content with a conditional className that changes background color based on the isActive state.
steps.hint: Use a ternary operator to set className to 'active' when isActive is true, and 'inactive' otherwise. Add this div as the outermost element in your return statement.
steps.analogousExample: // Conditional styling example div className={isOn ? 'light-on' : 'light-off'}>Content here
steps.expectedOutcome: The main container div will have dynamic styling that changes background color when the toggle button is clicked.
successCriteria: A div wrapper with conditional className based on isActive state is added around all existing content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added a div wrapper with a className that uses the isActive state in a ternary expression.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional styling wasn't implemented correctly. Check that you've added a div wrapper with className={isActive ? 'active' : 'inactive'} around your existing content.
